What Is a Go-to-Market Strategy?

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 17 November 2026 · 5-minute read · Strategy

In short: A go-to-market (GTM) strategy is the plan for how a company finds customers, persuades them to buy and does so at a cost that leaves a profitable business. lowob treats it as four decisions that must agree with each other: who exactly the buyer is, what they must believe, how trust moves from first contact to contract, and what evidence will show it is working. A list of channels and campaigns is not a GTM strategy; it is a list of tactics.

Key points

  • Gartner defines a GTM strategy as a plan that details how an organisation can engage with customers, and lists five components from target market to voice of the customer.
  • McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse found buyers use an average of ten interaction channels, up from five in 2016.
  • In Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, 61% said they prefer an overall rep-free buying experience.
  • A GTM strategy is a set of linked choices; changing the buyer changes the message, the path and the measures.
  • It should be written down, owned and revisited when evidence contradicts it, like any other commercial decision.

What a go-to-market strategy means

The term covers the commercial choices that sit between having a product and having revenue. Gartner's framework for sales leaders defines it as "a plan that details how an organization can engage with customers" and names five components: target market identification, the first customer touchpoint, sales compensation planning, corporate investments and voice of the customer.

lowob's working definition, set out in What Go-to-Market Means, groups the choices into four decisions. Each constrains the others.

DecisionQuestion it answersEvidence it is right
Who, exactlyWhich narrowly defined buyers have the costliest version of the problem, the authority and budget to fix it, and a reason to act now?Win rates and sales cycle by segment
What they must believeWhat change does the buyer want, in their own language?Buyers repeat the message back; loss reasons shift
How trust movesWhat is the path from first contact to signed contract: self-serve, sales-led, partner-led or community-led?Conversion and cost at each step of the path
What proves itWhich few numbers will show the strategy is working, and by when?Agreed targets, reviewed on a fixed rhythm

A GTM strategy is not the same as a marketing plan, a sales target or a product launch. Those are parts of it. The strategy is the agreement between the parts.

Why it matters for a commercial team

Buyers have changed the path

The third decision, how trust moves, has become harder. McKinsey's B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers, published in September 2024, found buyers used an average of ten channels in their buying journey, up from five in 2016. It also found a "rule of thirds": at each stage, roughly a third of buyers prefer in-person contact, a third remote contact and a third digital self-service.

Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, run in August and September 2024, found 61% prefer an overall rep-free buying experience. The same research found 73% avoid suppliers who send irrelevant outreach. A strategy that assumes every buyer wants a sales call, or that more outbound volume will compensate for a weak fit, now fails faster.

Tactics without a strategy waste money

Without the four decisions written down, each team picks its own. Marketing targets one segment, sales chases another and partners bring a third. Spending rises while win rates stay flat. lowob's piece on strategy versus tactics sets out the symptoms in more detail.

A go-to-market strategy is four choices that agree. Change one and the other three must be checked.

Agents need it written down

AI agents in sales and marketing amplify whatever strategy they are given. An outbound agent pointed at a loose ideal customer profile sends more messages to the wrong people, faster. In lowob's model, the GTM choices belong in the decision record, with a reason, owner and expected outcome, so agents and people read the same version.

How to test your go-to-market strategy

TestQuestion to ask the leadership teamWarning sign
Single buyerCan three leaders describe the target buyer in the same words?Three different answers
NarrownessCould a seller name ten real accounts that fit, today?"Mid-market companies"
BeliefDo win-loss interviews repeat your message?Buyers cite price or relationships only
Primary motionIs one path primary, with others in support?Every channel funded equally
EconomicsDo you know the cost to acquire a customer through the main path?Nobody owns the number
ReviewWhen did the strategy last change because of evidence?Never, or every month

Firms between 20 and 500 people usually run more than one motion. That is workable if one is primary and the others support it. Product-Led vs Sales-Led vs Partner-Led Growth covers how to choose.

lowob takeaways

  • Four decisions. Who, what they must believe, how trust moves and what proves it.
  • They must agree. A new segment means a new message, path and set of measures.
  • The path is harder. Buyers use more channels and many prefer to buy without a seller.
  • Write it down. Recorded choices keep teams, and agents, working from one version.

Common questions

What are the components of a go-to-market strategy?

Most frameworks cover the target buyer, the value proposition or message, the channels and sales motion, pricing and the measures of success. lowob groups these into four decisions that must agree.

What is the difference between a go-to-market strategy and a marketing strategy?

A marketing strategy covers how a company creates demand. A GTM strategy is wider: it also covers which buyers to pursue, how the sale happens and how success is measured across sales, marketing and partners.

How often should a go-to-market strategy change?

When evidence contradicts it, such as win rates falling in the target segment or a new path proving cheaper. Review it quarterly; change it less often.

Do B2B buyers still want to talk to salespeople?

Many prefer not to for much of the journey. Gartner found 61% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience overall, and McKinsey found preferences split roughly evenly between in-person, remote and self-service.

Sources and notes

  • Gartner, Go-To-Market Strategy Framework. Analyst framework page aimed at chief sales officers.
  • McKinsey, Five fundamental truths: How B2B winners keep growing, 12 September 2024. Consultancy survey of nearly 4,000 B2B decision makers.
  • Gartner, Gartner Sales Survey Finds 61% of B2B Buyers Prefer a Rep-Free Buying Experience, 25 June 2025. Analyst survey of 632 buyers, fielded in 2024.
